title: Characterization of blood culture-positive infectious episodes in children and adolescents undergoing chemotherapy
summary:
Background: Children and adolescents with cancer, as well as patients undergoing stem cell transplantation, have a particularly high risk of infections. Bacterial infections in particular can become dangerous. Despite major advances in cancer treatment, severe infections and sepsis are still among the most common causes of serious illness and death. That’s why it’s really important to detect a bacterial infection as early as possible and treat it quickly with antibiotics. The risk of a serious infection is especially high when the number of white blood cells (neutrophils), which are important for fighting off pathogens, is greatly reduced and this condition lasts for a long time. Other factors include the type of cancer, the intensity of chemotherapy, and individual patient characteristics. An additional problem is the increasing spread of bacteria that are resistant to antibiotics.  Infections with such pathogens more often lead to severe courses of illness, treatment in the intensive care unit, and higher mortality. Since the frequency of antibiotic-resistant germs differs significantly between hospitals, the responsible use of antibiotics and effective hygiene measures are particularly important. Study aim: This paper aims to investigate infections in children and adolescents who were treated during chemotherapy at the University Hospital RWTH Aachen and in whom bacteria were detected in the blood. The study will examine: - Which bacteria caused the infections. - Which risk factors favor the occurrence of a bloodstream infection. - Whether infections differ in patients with and without a deficiency of white blood cells (neutropenia). The results should help identify high-risk patients earlier and improve preventive as well as therapeutic measures. Main objective: Description of bloodstream infections in children and adolescents with a positive blood culture during chemotherapy at the University Hospital RWTH Aachen. Secondary objectives: - Recording the different pathogens and their antibiotic resistances. - Investigation of patient-related risk factors for bloodstream infections. - Analysis of the connection between the underlying disease, the intensity of treatment, and the causative pathogens. - Investigation of the consequences of the infections, for example: - Stay in the intensive care unit, - Duration of hospital stay, - Recurrent infections, - Mortality. - Assessment of the influence of neutropenia and the presence of a central venous catheter on the occurrence of bloodstream infections. Study assumptions (hypotheses): Patients with severe neutropenia more frequently have bloodstream infections caused by gram-negative bacteria. The presence of a central venous catheter increases the risk of certain catheter-associated infections, especially those caused by so-called coagulase-negative staphylococci. Patients during particularly intensive phases of chemotherapy are more likely to develop severe infections. Infections with antibiotic-resistant bacteria more often lead to longer hospital stays and are associated with higher mortality. Procedure For the study, data from a defined group of patients will be analyzed. The required information comes from patient records, the hospital information system MEDICO, and the HYBASE database of the Central Department of Hospital Hygiene and Infectiology. The data from a period of ten years will be examined. 

In short: The study looks at which bacteria cause bloodstream infections in children and adolescents under chemotherapy, which risk factors are responsible, and what consequences these infections have. The goal is to improve the prevention, detection, and treatment of such infections in the future.
conditions: Personal history of chemotherapy for neoplastic disease
Condition after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation with current immunosuppression

interventions.name: Monocentric retrospective analysis of infection events in pediatric patients (0 to <18 years) with positive blood cultures who received chemotherapy at the University Hospital Aachen. The goal is on one hand to classify the pathogens identified, and on the other, to determine clinical risk factors f

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Treatment in the Clinic for Pediatrics and Adolescent Medicine at UKA
- underlying oncological condition and/or stem cell transplantation
- ongoing or recently completed chemotherapy
- at least one positive blood culture during the study period
Exclusion criteria:
- Patients without chemotherapy
- exclusively contaminated blood cultures without clinical relevance
- incomplete datasets with missing core data
